chmmc-2017-team-01.title: Parity, then factor
chmmc-2017-team-01.body:
The sum is a prime larger than $2$, hence odd, so exactly one of the four primes is $2$. If $2\in\{q,r,s\}$, then $p^2+2k$ with $k$ an odd prime is $\equiv1+2\equiv3\pmod4$, never a square. So $p=2$.

Take $r<s$ and write $4+qr=m^2$, $4+qs=n^2$ ($m,n$ even, $m<n$). Then $qr=(m-2)(m+2)$ and $qs=(n-2)(n+2)$. Each factor is more than $1$, so $\{q,r\}=\{m-2,m+2\}$ and $\{q,s\}=\{n-2,n+2\}$. Since $m-2<n-2<n+2$ and $m+2<n+2$, we get $q=m+2=n-2$, so $r=q-4$, $s=q+4$. The numbers $q-4,q,q+4$ have distinct residues mod $3$, so one is divisible by $3$ and prime means it is $3$: $q-4=3$. So $(r,q,s)=(3,7,11)$ and the sum is $2+3+7+11=23$ (prime).

**Answer: 23**

chmmc-2017-team-02.title: Cases by length
chmmc-2017-team-02.body:
Put Adam at $(0,0)$, the goal at $(4,4)$, the crumb at $(1,1)$. A path has even length, at least $8$, and at most $10$ (energy $9$, or $10$ if he eats the crumb, which he must then do on the way).

**Length 8:** shortest paths, $\binom84=70$.

**Length 10.** The path must pass through $(1,1)$. Either he first reaches $(1,1)$ after $4$ steps ($8$ ways) and then takes a shortest path of $6$ steps to $(4,4)$ ($\binom63=20$ ways): $8\cdot20=160$. Or he first reaches $(1,1)$ in $2$ steps ($2$ ways) and then walks $8$ steps to $(4,4)$ using one backward step: $3$ ups, $4$ rights and $1$ left, or the mirror image. For one type there are $\binom83$ choices for the up-steps and $4$ positions for the left step (it must precede the last right step); we subtract the $\binom63$ walks ending with left-then-right, which would already have reached $(4,4)$ earlier. This gives $2\cdot2\left(4\binom83-\binom63\right)=816$.

Total $70+160+816=1046$.

**Answer: 1046**

chmmc-2017-team-02.title: Computer enumeration
chmmc-2017-team-02.body:
A depth-first enumeration of all walks on the $5\times5$ lattice of points, tracking energy (including the one-time crumb at $(1,1)$) and stopping at $(4,4)$, counts exactly $1046$ walks.

**Answer: 1046**

chmmc-2017-team-03.title: Space-time picture
chmmc-2017-team-03.body:
Draw the position of every bus against time; Dirk follows a bus until its line crosses a bus going the other way, then switches to that line. Following the crossings (first meetings at $0.125$ h, $7.5$ mi, then back at $0.375$ h, $2.5$ mi, then forward to $0.5$ h, $10$ mi, ...) one finds that Dirk first reaches the point $10n$ miles from Town $A$ exactly $\frac{3n}{2}-1$ hours after noon. For $n=10$ (Town $B$) this is $\frac{30}{2}-1=14$ hours.

**Answer: 14 hours**

chmmc-2017-team-03.title: Exact simulation
chmmc-2017-team-03.body:
Simulating the whole process with exact fractions (always take the earliest meeting with an oncoming bus, switch direction, and stop when the forward bus reaches $B$ before meeting another bus) gives arrival at exactly $14$ hours after noon.

**Answer: 14 hours**

chmmc-2017-team-04.title: Telescoping
chmmc-2017-team-04.body:
Looking at powers of $2$ mod $5$ and mod $17$: $a^{2^j}$ runs through $a,a^2,a^4,a^3$ (repeating, period 4) and $b^{2^j}$ through $b,b^2,b^4,b^8,b^{16},b^{15},b^{13},b^9$ (period 8). So the eight factors are, in a different order, $\prod_{j=0}^{7}\left(a^{2^j}+b^{2^j}\right)$ (the pairs match: $a^3\leftrightarrow b^8$, $a^3\leftrightarrow b^9=b^{2^7}$ etc.). Since $a^{2^j}+b^{2^j}=\dfrac{a^{2^{j+1}}-b^{2^{j+1}}}{a^{2^j}-b^{2^j}}$, the product telescopes to $\dfrac{a^{256}-b^{256}}{a-b}$. Now $a^5=1$ and $256\equiv1\pmod5$, and $b^{17}=1$ with $256=15\cdot17+1$, so $a^{256}=a$, $b^{256}=b$ and the value is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

chmmc-2017-team-05.title: Union of all four, minus unchosen pairs
chmmc-2017-team-05.body:
Moving a point along its radius does not change whether it lies on the same side of lines through the center, so we may place the four points on the circle. The union of the four triangles is the convex hull of the points. It misses the center iff all four points lie in a semicircle, which has probability $4\cdot\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac12$. So the center is in the hull with probability $\frac12$.

A point not on any side lies in either $0$ or $2$ of the four triangles (when it is in the hull). So the center, when in the hull, lies in exactly one pair-intersection, and these $6$ events are equally likely: probability $\frac{1/2}{6}=\frac1{12}$ each. The center lies in the union of the two chosen triangles iff it is in the hull but not in the intersection of the two unchosen triangles (those two triangles have the other two as complement). The probability is $\frac12-\frac1{12}=\frac5{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac5{12}$**

chmmc-2017-team-05.title: Simulation
chmmc-2017-team-05.body:
A Monte Carlo simulation of $4\times10^5$ trials gives $0.4163$, in agreement with $\frac5{12}=0.4167$.

**Answer: $\frac5{12}$**

chmmc-2017-team-06.title: Cycles with trees
chmmc-2017-team-06.body:
Each component of the directed graph is a cycle (length at least $2$, since there are no loops) with rooted trees hanging off it.

*One component.* Cycle of length $5$: $1$ graph. Length $4$: $1$. Length $3$ with two further vertices: either both point to the same cycle vertex, or they form a path off one cycle vertex, or one hangs off each of two cycle vertices: $3$ graphs. Length $2$ with three further vertices: the trees on the two cycle vertices have sizes $\{1,4\}$ (there are $4$ rooted trees on $4$ vertices, so $4$ graphs) or $\{2,3\}$ ($1\cdot2=2$ graphs). Total $1+1+3+4+2=11$.

*Several components.* Each needs at least $2$ vertices, so exactly two components with $2$ and $3$ vertices: the $2$-vertex one is a $2$-cycle, the $3$-vertex one is a $3$-cycle or a $2$-cycle with a tail: $2$ graphs.

Total $11+2=13$.

**Answer: 13**

chmmc-2017-team-06.title: Computer count
chmmc-2017-team-06.body:
Enumerating all $4^5=1024$ fixed-point-free maps on $\{1,\dots,5\}$ and identifying isomorphic ones under all $120$ relabelings leaves exactly $13$ classes.

**Answer: 13**

chmmc-2017-team-07.title: Similar triangles and power of a point
chmmc-2017-team-07.body:
By tangent-chord, $\angle BAX=\angle BCA$, so $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle XBA$ with ratio $BC/AB=2$. Hence $BX=\frac{AB}2=9$ and $AX=\frac{CA}2=12$. Let $D=AY\cap BC$. By the angle bisector theorem in $\triangle AXC$ ($XC=27$, $AX=12$, $AC=24$): $XD:DC=12:24$, so $DX=9$, $DC=18$. Put $d=AD$, $y=AY$. Power of a point: $d(y-d)=9\cdot18=162$. Also $\triangle AXY\sim\triangle ADC$ gives $\frac{12}{d}=\frac{y}{24}$, i.e. $dy=288$. Subtracting, $d^2=288-162=126$, $d=3\sqrt{14}$, so $y=\frac{288}{3\sqrt{14}}=\frac{48\sqrt{14}}{7}$. Thus $p+q+r=48+7+14=69$.

**Answer: 69**

chmmc-2017-team-07.title: Coordinates check
chmmc-2017-team-07.body:
With $A=(0,0)$, $B=(18,0)$, $C$ determined by $CA=24$, $CB=36$, the circle is centered on the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$. Computing $X$ and the bisector direction numerically gives $AY=25.6571\ldots=\frac{48\sqrt{14}}7$.

**Answer: 69**

chmmc-2017-team-08.title: Recurrence
chmmc-2017-team-08.body:
Let $f_n$ be the polynomial of degree at most $n$ with $f_n(k)=k!$ for $0\le k\le n$ and $T_n=f_n(n+1)$. The polynomial $g(x)=f_n(x)-xf_{n-1}(x-1)$ has degree at most $n$ and vanishes at $x=1,\dots,n$, so $g(x)=c(x-1)\cdots(x-n)$. From $g(0)=f_n(0)=1$ we get $c=\frac{(-1)^n}{n!}$. Evaluating at $x=n+1$: $T_n=(-1)^n+(n+1)T_{n-1}$. With $T_1=1$: $T_2=4,T_3=15,T_4=76,T_5=455,T_6=3186$.

**Answer: 3186**

chmmc-2017-team-08.title: Finite differences
chmmc-2017-team-08.body:
A polynomial of degree at most $6$ has vanishing $7$th difference: $\sum_{k=0}^{7}(-1)^{7-k}\binom7kP(k)=0$. Hence $P(7)=\sum_{k=0}^{6}(-1)^{6-k}\binom7k\,k!=5040-2520+840-210+42-7+1=3186$.

**Answer: 3186**

chmmc-2017-team-09.title: Linearity of expectation
chmmc-2017-team-09.body:
Let there be $n-1$ numbers $1,\dots,n-1$ ($n=32$) and include $0$ as the start/end point. For each ordered pair $i\ne j$ in $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the trip goes directly $i\to j$ with probability $\frac1{n-1}$ (the route is a uniformly random cyclic order through $0$). So $E=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i,j}|i-j|=\frac{2}{n-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}\ell(n-\ell)=\frac2{n-1}\binom{n+1}3=\frac{n(n+1)}3$. With $n=32$: $\frac{32\cdot33}3=352$.

**Answer: 352**

chmmc-2017-team-09.title: Check small cases
chmmc-2017-team-09.body:
Exact computation for $n-1=3,5,7$ numbers gives $\frac{20}3,14,24$, matching $\frac{n(n+1)}3$ for $n=4,6,8$.

**Answer: 352**

chmmc-2017-team-10.title: Track the images of monotone pieces
chmmc-2017-team-10.body:
From $\alpha(\alpha-1)^2=1$ we get $(\alpha^2-\alpha)^2=\alpha$. So the orbit of $0$ is $0\to-\alpha\to\alpha^2-\alpha\to0$, i.e. $p_3(0)=0$ (a double root there). Cut $\mathbb R$ into intervals on which $p_n$ is monotone and whose image is one of $[0,\infty)$, $[-\alpha,0]$, $[0,\alpha^2-\alpha]$; let $x_n,y_n,z_n$ count the intervals of each type. Under $p_{n+1}=p_n^2-\alpha$: $[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)+[-\alpha,0]$, $[-\alpha,0]\to[-\alpha,0]+[0,\alpha^2-\alpha]$, $[0,\alpha^2-\alpha]\to[-\alpha,0]$. So $x_{n+1}=x_n$, $y_{n+1}=x_n+y_n+z_n$, $z_{n+1}=y_n$ with $x_1=2,y_1=2,z_1=0$, giving $x_n=2$ and $y_n=2F_{n+2}-2$ (Fibonacci numbers). Each root lies in exactly two intervals (endpoints), so the number of real roots is $\frac{x_n+y_n+z_n}2=F_{n+3}-1$ for $n\ge2$. For $n=10$: $F_{13}-1=233-1=232$.

**Answer: 232**

chmmc-2017-team-10.title: Direct count of preimages
chmmc-2017-team-10.body:
Solving $p_{10}(x)=0$ backwards: start from the value set $\{0\}$ and repeatedly replace each value $y$ by $\pm\sqrt{y+\alpha}$ (discarding $y<-\alpha$ and merging coincident values, which occurs at $y=-\alpha$ where the square root is $0$). Doing this ten times in high precision leaves exactly $232$ distinct values.

**Answer: 232**
